title: WindBorne’s AI beats the government’s weather forecasts. Making money from them is the harder problem
excerpt: WindBorne raised a $37M Series B at a $250M valuation. Its balloons and AI model out-forecast government agencies. Selling that is the harder part.
content_html:
WindBorne Systems has raised $37 million to sell something it has already proven it can build: weather forecasts that beat the government’s. The Series B, reported by TechCrunch, was co-led by Khosla Ventures and Galvanize and values the company at $250 million. It takes WindBorne’s total funding past $62 million.

The forecasting is the easy part now. Turning it into a business is the hard one.

The planetary nervous system

WindBorne flies balloons. About 600 of them are in the air at any moment, launched from 20 sites worldwide. They drift for weeks, gathering readings where satellites and weather stations cannot. The eye of a typhoon is one such place. The company calls the network a planetary nervous system, and it is the point of the whole business.

That data feeds WeatherMesh, WindBorne’s AI forecasting model. The latest version, released two months ago, tops public benchmarks as the most accurate weather model available. It beats the leading AI systems and the traditional physics-based models that governments run. It does so on far less computing power to train.

The moat is the data, not the model. Anyone can train a forecasting AI on public datasets. WindBorne also owns readings nobody else has. “The value per data point is much stronger than satellites,” chief executive John Dean told TechCrunch. Growing revenue while proving it, he added, “de-risked the demand signal to VCs.”

Sold to the government, betting on business

For now, WindBorne’s customers are mostly public. The US National Weather Service buys its data. The Air Force and Navy pay through research partnerships, including work on forecasting models that can run onboard ships with patchy connections. Its readings are already folded into NOAA’s Global Forecast System, one of the backbones of everyday weather apps.

The growth bet points the other way, at the private sector. Trading firms and investment funds were the earliest commercial takers, using sharper forecasts to price commodities and weather-sensitive markets. Expanding that base is what the new money is for. The round also funds more compute and a mesh radio network to replace the balloons’ satellite links. It even pays for ocean buoys that keep sensing after they splash down.

Why this is the hard part

Selling sensing data to businesses has broken startups before. Earth-observing satellite networks spent a decade trying and mostly retreated to government buyers. Extracting value from raw data takes workflows and expertise most companies lack. Private weather firms have survived by repackaging government forecasts, de-icing planes, routing ships, and serving speculators.

WindBorne’s bet is that AI changes the maths. “Integrating weather forecasts into broader business decision-making has traditionally been expensive and difficult,” said Galvanize’s Saloni Multani, who co-led the round. Better forecasts make the effort worthwhile, she argued, and AI makes wiring them into decisions far easier. “We think AI changes that equation.”

The backers are betting on the pairing. Khosla Ventures, fresh from co-leading Jeff Dean’s new AI venture, has held its stake since the first cheque. “As AI models become increasingly capable, the quality of the underlying observations becomes even more important,” said Khosla’s Sven Strohband. WindBorne also fits a wider pattern: investors pouring capital into AI bound to the physical world, from autonomous mining to fusion power.

The demand is not in doubt. Extreme weather is getting more frequent and more expensive, and the appetite for early warning is growing on both sides of the public-private line. The question WindBorne has to answer is the one every sensing startup before it hit. Whether better data, this time wrapped in AI, is finally something enough customers will pay for.

content_html_zh:
WindBorne Systems 已筹集 3700 万美元，用于出售其已证明可以打造的产品：优于政府的天气预报。 据 TechCrunch 报道，B 轮融资由 Khosla Ventures 和 Galvanize 共同领投，该公司估值为 2.5 亿美元。 WindBorne 的总融资额已超过 6200 万美元。

现在预测是比较容易的部分。 将其转变为一项业务是困难的。

行星神经系统

WindBorne 飞行气球。 其中约 600 架随时从全球 20 个地点发射。 它们漂流数周，收集卫星和气象站无法收集的读数。 台风眼就是这样一个地方。 该公司称网络为行星神经系统，是整个业务的重点。

这些数据为 WindBorne 的 AI 预测模型 WeatherMesh 提供数据。 两个月前发布的最新版本超越了公共基准，成为最准确的天气模型。 它击败了领先的人工智能系统和政府运行的传统的基于物理的模型。 它的训练计算能力要少得多。

护城河是数据，而不是模型。 任何人都可以在公共数据集上训练预测人工智能。 WindBorne 还拥有其他人没有的读数。 “每个数据点的价值比卫星强得多，”首席执行官约翰·迪恩 (John Dean) 告诉 TechCrunch。 他补充说，在证明这一点的同时，收入的增长“降低了风险投资的需求信号的风险。”

卖给政府，赌生意

目前，WindBorne 的客户主要是公众。 美国国家气象局购买其数据。 空军和海军通过研究合作伙伴关系支付费用，包括研究可以在连接不完整的舰船上运行的预测模型。 它的读数已经被纳入 NOAA 的全球预报系统，这是日常天气应用​​程序的支柱之一。

增长押注指向另一个方向，即私营部门。 贸易公司和投资基金是最早的商业接受者，利用更准确的预测来为大宗商品和天气敏感市场定价。 新资金的目的就是扩大这一基础。 该轮融资还资助更多的计算和网状无线电网络，以取代气球的卫星链路。 它甚至还支付了在溅落后保持感应的海洋浮标的费用。

为什么这是最困难的部分

向企业出售传感数据曾让初创企业陷入困境。 地球观测卫星网络花了十年的时间进行尝试，但大部分都退给了政府买家。 从原始数据中提取价值需要大多数公司所缺乏的工作流程和专业知识。 私营气象公司通过重新包装政府预报、为飞机除冰、为船舶航线和为投机者提供服务而生存下来。

WindBorne 的赌注是人工智能会改变数学。 “传统上，将天气预报纳入更广泛的商业决策是昂贵且困难的，”本轮联合牵头人、Galvanize 的萨罗尼·穆尔塔尼 (Saloni Multani) 表示。 她认为，更好的预测会让付出的努力变得值得，而人工智能则让预测变得更加容易。 “我们认为人工智能改变了这个方程式。”

支持者押注于这对搭档。 科斯拉风险投资公司 (Khosla Ventures) 刚刚联合领导杰夫·迪恩 (Jeff Dean) 的新人工智能企业，自第一张支票以来就一直持有其股份。 “随着人工智能模型的能力越来越强，基础观察的质量变得更加重要，”科斯拉的斯文·斯特罗班德说。 WindBorne 也符合更广泛的模式：投资者将资金投入到与物理世界相关的人工智能领域，从自主采矿到核聚变发电。

需求是毫无疑问的。 极端天气变得越来越频繁，成本也越来越高，公私双方对预警的需求都在增长。 WindBorne 必须回答的问题是每一个传感初创公司在上市之前都会遇到的问题。 这次包含在人工智能中的更好的数据是否最终会成为足够多的客户愿意付费的东西。
